...         "target": ["H", "K", "C", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> spec.layer_nodes[1]
('H', 'K')
>>> spec.unit_index(["K", "H"], layer=1)
(1, 0)

A node of width 3 gives its whole block, and every node of a layer gives every unit of that layer:

>>> wide = kpnn2.parse_layered(
...     edgelist,
...     widths={"H": 3},
... )
>>> wide.unit_index(["K", "H"], layer=1)
(3, 0, 1, 2)
>>> wide.unit_index(wide.layer_nodes[1], layer=1) == tuple(
...     range(wide.layer_dims[1])
... )
True

As a buffer, it reads those units from that layer's tensor:

>>> index = torch.as_tensor(
...     wide.unit_index(["K"], layer=1),
...     dtype=torch.int64,
... )
>>> saved = {1: torch.arange(4.0).unsqueeze(0)}
>>> saved[1][..., index].tolist()
[[3.0]]

docs.title: node_table
docs.text:
node_table() -> pd.DataFrame

Return one row of graph counts per node.

Each row says where a node sits in the graph: its layer, how many units it owns, how many edges enter and leave it, and how many nodes reach it or are reached from it. A node with many connections tends to get large sums and large scores only because it is large, so these counts are what such a node is scaled by: a widths value set from its number of parents, a division of its input by its in-degree in forward(), or a check of whether node scores follow connectivity. The table holds the raw counts; the formula stays yours.

Counts are over named edges in the direction of computation, so widths never change them. An input that feeds a node, directly or through other nodes, is one of its ancestors. The table is computed on each call and is a new DataFrame each time, so changing it does not change this spec.

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

Index node: every node name in unit order, layer by layer and alphabetical within a layer (the flattened layer_nodes). Columns, all int64:

  • layer: the node's layer in layer_nodes
  • width: the number of units the node owns
  • in_degree: edges into the node, one per parent
  • out_degree: edges out of the node, one per child
  • n_ancestors: other nodes with a path to the node
  • n_descendants: other nodes the node has a path to
  • n_input_ancestors: how many of its ancestors are in input_nodes
See Also

to_edgelist : The named edges the counts are taken over. node_units : One node's unit slice on its layer.

Notes

in_degree == 0 selects exactly input_nodes, and out_degree == 0 exactly output_nodes. Rows follow unit order, so numpy.repeat(table[column], table["width"]) gives one value per unit, layer after layer; filter table[table["layer"] == i] first for the units of layer i. When counts should set widths, read them from a first parse without widths: they count named edges, so the second parse has the same counts.

Examples:

Three inputs feed two hidden nodes, which feed y; x3 also feeds y directly:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["x1", "x2", "x2", "x3", "h1", "h2", "x3"],
...         "target": ["h1", "h1", "h2", "h2", "y", "y", "y"],
...     }
... )
>>> table = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist).node_table()
>>> table[["layer", "width", "in_degree", "out_degree"]]
      layer  width  in_degree  out_degree
node
x1        0      1          0           1
x2        0      1          0           2
x3        0      1          0           2
h1        1      1          2           1
h2        1      1          2           1
y         2      1          3           0
>>> table[["n_ancestors", "n_descendants", "n_input_ancestors"]]
      n_ancestors  n_descendants  n_input_ancestors
node
x1              0              2                  0
x2              0              3                  0
x3              0              2                  0
h1              2              1                  2
h2              2              1                  2
y               5              0                  3

A wider node keeps its counts, and repeating a column by width gives one value per unit:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> wide = kpnn2.parse_layered(
...     edgelist,
...     widths={"h1": 2},
... ).node_table()
>>> wide.loc["h1", ["width", "in_degree"]].tolist()
[2, 2]
>>> np.repeat(wide["in_degree"], wide["width"]).tolist()
[0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2, 3]

docs.title: to_dict
docs.text:
to_dict() -> dict

Return this spec as a JSON-safe tagged dict.

Keys are kpnn2_spec (integer 1), layout ("layered"), and edges (list of [source, target] lists in the same order as to_edgelist() rows). When any node has width other than 1, a "widths" object of those names is included. All-1 graphs omit "widths". When compacted layers differ from longest-path on the same edges, a "ranks" object maps every node to its compacted 0-based layer index. A ranks= parse that matches longest-path omits "ranks". The returned dict is new on every call.

Returns:

Type Description dict

Tagged edge list plus layout.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["A", "H"],
...         "target": ["H", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> payload = spec.to_dict()
>>> payload["kpnn2_spec"]
1
>>> payload["layout"]
'layered'
>>> payload["edges"]
[['A', 'H'], ['H', 'C']]

docs.title: from_dict classmethod
docs.text:
from_dict(payload: dict) -> LayeredSpec

Rebuild a LayeredSpec from to_dict() output.

Calls parse_layered on a DataFrame built from payload["edges"], passing payload["widths"] and payload["ranks"] when present. Hops and packed indices are not assembled by hand. Extra unknown keys are ignored. An absent or empty "widths" object is width 1. Absent "ranks" is longest-path.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dict

A dict with kpnn2_spec, layout, and edges. layout must be "layered". Optional "widths" is a node-name-to-int object. Optional "ranks" is a node-name-to-int object of compacted (or user) depths.

required

Returns:

Type Description LayeredSpec

The parsed spec.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If payload is not a dict; kpnn2_spec is missing or not 1; layout is missing, not a known layout, or is "adjacency"; edges is missing or not a sequence of two nonempty names, or a name is not a str, integer, float, or bool; "widths" is present and not a mapping of positive integers; or "ranks" is present and not a mapping of non-negative integers covering every node.

Warns:

Type Description UserWarning

If an edge name is a float or a bool, as in parse_layered.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["A", "H"],
...         "target": ["H", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> roundtrip = kpnn2.LayeredSpec.from_dict(spec.to_dict())
>>> roundtrip.layer_nodes == spec.layer_nodes
True

docs.title: MaskedLinear
docs.text:
MaskedLinear(
    mask: Tensor,
    bias: bool = True,
    *,
    identity: str | None = None,
    constraint: Module | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
)

Bases: Module

Affine hop whose connectivity is fixed by an edgelist mask.

One hop of a knowledge-primed network: an nn.Linear-style layer (call layer(x); not a subclass) in which only edges present in the prior-knowledge graph can carry weight, so absent edges need no hand-zeroing after every optimizer step. Build one from spec.hops[i].to_mask() or spec.to_mask(), fed by gather_hop_inputs on a layered hop. The large-n path on the same indices is PackedLinear, which stores its weight the same way: weight is the trainable tensor and effective_weight() is what forward uses. Initialization scales by per-row mask degree.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default Tensor

Connectivity of shape (out_features, in_features), usually spec.hops[i].to_mask() or spec.to_mask(). Every entry is 0 or 1: a 1 at [j, k] lets input column k reach output row j; a 0 blocks it for the life of the layer. Bool, integer, and floating dtypes are accepted. Both dimensions must be at least 1, and at least one entry must be 1; all-zero rows and columns are allowed. Per-edge scaling or signs belong in constraint, not in the mask. Stored as an independent float32 copy, so later writes to the tensor passed in do not reach this layer.

required bool

If True, learn a bias of shape (out_features,). If False, there is no bias. Must be a bool.

True str or None

Opaque checkpoint identity, typically spec.fingerprint. Stored in state_dict next to mask_digest as a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of the UTF-8 bytes. load_state_dict compares it with the checkpoint's identity:

  • the checkpoint has no identity: it loads, even with strict=True
  • it has this layer's identity: it loads
  • it has another identity, or this layer's identity is None: Kpnn2Error, and no weights are loaded

None means this layer does not claim an identity, so it loads only checkpoints saved without one.

None Module or None

Optional per-entry map on weight, applied in forward before the mask. The module must return a tensor of the same shape as weight. Give it a right_inverse (the torch.nn.utils.parametrize convention) and reset_parameters stores right_inverse(draw), so the effective weight keeps the degree-aware init; without one, weight stores the draw and the map is applied on top of it. nn.Softplus() is the textbook non-negative edge reparametrization but has no right_inverse: every live edge then starts near ln 2 whatever its fan-in (see Notes). PackedLinear takes the same argument. Mixed per-edge signs and frozen slots belong in this module, not in parse columns. A hard freeze is torch.where replacing those slots; a gradient hook that zeroes a slot is not a freeze (AdamW and SGD with momentum still move the stored tensor).

None Generator or None

Isolated RNG for reset_parameters. None uses the default torch generator, bit-identical to omitting the argument. Not stored on the module; pass it again to reset_parameters to replay. Do not pass a seed integer.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description in_features int

Number of input columns, mask.shape[1].

out_features int

Number of output columns, mask.shape[0].

weight Parameter

The trainable tensor, shape (out_features, in_features), stored under the name weight as on nn.Linear. Masked-out entries start at exactly 0; their gradient is always 0, so SGD, momentum, Adam, and weight decay keep them at 0. When constraint is set, this tensor is unconstrained. Read effective_weight() for the map forward uses.

mask Tensor

Float32 buffer, same shape as the constructor mask. Not trained and not saved in state_dict. Stays float32 after .half() / bfloat16 / .double(). Treat it as read-only: like any PyTorch buffer it can be written to, and doing so silently rewires the layer. Rebuild from the edgelist instead.

constraint Module or None

The constructor constraint module, or None.

bias Parameter | None

Trainable bias, or None when constructed with bias=False.

identity str | None

The constructor identity, or None.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If mask is not a torch.Tensor or is not 2-D; if mask has a dimension of size 0, has a complex dtype, holds a value other than 0 and 1 (NaN included), or has no entry equal to 1; if bias is not a bool; if identity is neither a str nor None; if constraint is neither an nn.Module nor None, or does not preserve the weight shape; if generator is neither a torch.Generator nor None; from load_state_dict when the checkpoint carries a mask digest or identity that does not match this layer, in which case the weights are not loaded; and from forward when x is not a floating-point tensor or its last dimension is not in_features.

See Also

PackedLinear : One trainable scalar per live edge, for graphs whose dense (out_features, in_features) weight would not fit in RAM. Tied decode is PackedLinear.transpose; on this layer use F.linear(h, layer.effective_weight().T, dec_bias). gather_hop_inputs : Assembles the input tensor of a hop that reads more than one saved layer. torch.nn.Linear : Dense equivalent, and the reference for shapes, bias, calling the module, and training.

Notes

Sizes come from mask.shape; there are no separate size arguments. Forward is Y = F.linear(X, effective_weight(), bias), that is Y = X @ (C(W) ⊙ M).T + b with W the weight parameter, C the constraint (the identity when omitted), and M the mask cast to W's dtype and device, so .half(), bfloat16, and .double() work as on nn.Linear. torch.autocast is unsupported: forward disables it and casts a floating x to the parameter dtype; an integer, bool, or complex x raises instead of being cast. The multiply is dense on purpose, and X is an ordinary dense activation tensor. Nothing in the forward path is a tensor subclass, so torch.compile(layer, fullgraph=True) traces it.

The mask is always applied last. A map you register_parametrization on weight yourself runs when weight is read, before constraint and before the mask, so it cannot resurrect a blocked entry. constraint is the supported per-entry map for sign-constrained edges.

weight is a plain nn.Parameter, as on nn.Linear and PackedLinear:

  • state_dict keys are weight, optional bias, mask_digest, and identity when the constructor was given one; mask stays out of it. mask_digest is a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of length 32: the SHA-256 of the live mask's float32 C-contiguous bytes at save time, not a registered buffer. A missing digest is not an error, even with strict=True. The digest catches same-shape rewiring. A rename that leaves the 0/1 pattern unchanged is caught by identity when callers pass spec.fingerprint. A kpnn2 0.1 checkpoint, which stored the trainable tensor as parametrizations.weight.original, still loads; its masked-out entries are set to 0 on load, which does not change the output.
  • Param-group filters match weight the same way on this layer, PackedLinear, and nn.Linear.
  • copy.deepcopy and pickling (torch.save(model)) work.
  • torch.nn.utils.prune works on weight; its mask composes with the connectivity mask.

weight is the unconstrained tensor, so optimizer weight_decay pulls it toward 0. Under softplus that pulls the effective weight toward ln 2, not toward 0. Give a constrained layer weight_decay=0 in its param group and penalize effective_weight() in the loss instead. A right_inverse on the constraint keeps the degree-aware init; a constraint without one can initialize weight itself from init_bound().

reset_parameters uses per-row mask degree as fan_in, not full in_features. Because a hop carries every parent of its target, including skip parents, that per-row degree is the unit's real fan-in. Optional generator isolates those draws from other torch RNG consumers.

Examples:

One hop whose second output is connected only to the second input:

>>> import torch
>>> import kpnn2
>>> mask = torch.tensor(
...     [
...         [1.0, 1.0],
...         [0.0, 1.0],
...     ]
... )
>>> layer = kpnn2.MaskedLinear(
...     mask,
...     bias=False,
... )
>>> layer.in_features, layer.out_features
(2, 2)
>>> y = layer(torch.ones(3, 2))
>>> tuple(y.shape)
(3, 2)

weight is the trainable parameter; a blocked entry starts at 0 there and is 0 in the map forward uses:

>>> [name for name, _ in layer.named_parameters()]
['weight']
>>> bool(layer.weight[1, 0] == 0.0)
True
>>> bool(layer.effective_weight()[1, 0] == 0.0)
True

constraint is applied before the mask, so blocked entries stay zero even though softplus(0) > 0:

>>> layer = kpnn2.MaskedLinear(
...     mask,
...     bias=False,
...     constraint=torch.nn.Softplus(),
... )
>>> bool(layer.effective_weight()[1, 0] == 0.0)
True

docs.title: effective_weight
docs.text:
effective_weight() -> torch.Tensor

Return the (out_features, in_features) map forward uses.

constraint(weight) when constraint is set (else weight), times the mask cast to that tensor's dtype and device. Recomputed on every call and differentiable, so it is the tensor to read, export, or penalize as the layer's live edge weights. PackedLinear has the same method.

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The effective weight. Blocked entries are 0.

docs.title: init_bound
docs.text:
init_bound() -> torch.Tensor

Return the degree-aware init bound of every weight entry.

A live entry of row j gets 1 / sqrt(fan_in) of that row, the bound reset_parameters draws its effective weight from. Blocked entries, and rows with fan_in == 0, get 0. Use it to initialize a constraint that has no right_inverse yourself. PackedLinear has the same method on its packed slots.

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

Shape (out_features, in_features), dtype and device of weight.

docs.title: reset_parameters
docs.text:
reset_parameters(
    generator: Generator | None = None,
) -> None

Initialize from per-row mask degree, not full width.

This is the difference from torch.nn.Linear.reset_parameters. For output row j, fan_in is the number of ones in mask[j]. The live entries of that row of weight (and bias[j], if present) are drawn uniformly from [-1 / sqrt(fan_in), 1 / sqrt(fan_in)] (init_bound()). Masked-out entries are 0. If fan_in == 0, the row and bias entry stay 0.

Rows are drawn one at a time, each as a full row that is then masked, so the draws match earlier releases and no full-size temporary is allocated.

The draw is the degree-aware value for the effective weight. Without constraint, or when constraint has no right_inverse, weight stores the draw itself. When constraint defines right_inverse (the torch.nn.utils.parametrize convention), weight stores constraint.right_inverse(draw) on live entries (blocked entries stay 0), so effective_weight() keeps the degree-aware scale. The draws, and so the RNG stream, are the same either way.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default Generator or None

Isolated RNG for these draws. None uses the default torch generator. Not stored on the module.

None

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If generator is neither a torch.Generator nor None, or constraint.right_inverse returns a tensor of the wrong shape or a non-finite value on a live entry.

docs.title: forward
docs.text:
forward(x: Tensor) -> torch.Tensor

F.linear of x with effective_weight().

The constraint (if any) and then the mask are applied to weight here, on every call. The stored mask remains float32 and is cast to the parameter dtype, so .half(), bfloat16, and .double() match nn.Linear. torch.autocast is unsupported: this path disables it and casts x to the parameter dtype.

Raises Kpnn2Error when x is not a floating-point tensor or its last dimension is not in_features. An integer, bool, or complex x is rejected, not cast.

docs.title: PackedLinear
docs.text:
PackedLinear(
    source_index: object,
    target_index: object,
    out_features: int,
    in_features: int,
    bias: bool = True,
    *,
    identity: str | None = None,
    constraint: Module | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
)

Bases: Module

Affine map with one trainable scalar per live edge.

An nn.Linear-style layer (call layer(x); not a subclass, not a full model) for a graph laid out by parse_layered or parse_adjacency. On a hop it stores one weight per live edge of that hop instead of the dense (out, in) rectangle MaskedLinear(hop.to_mask()) would. On an AdjacencySpec it stores one weight per graph edge instead of an (n, n) square. Reach for it when that rectangle or square strains RAM. On an AdjacencySpec, input nodes have no incoming edges, so writing inputs into the state each step is the caller's job.

Build it with from_hop on a hop or from_adjacency on an AdjacencySpec: both read the indices and widths off the spec, so source and target cannot be swapped by hand. The constructor below takes packed indices directly, for pairs that come from no spec; transpose builds on it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default torch.Tensor, numpy.ndarray, or sequence of int

1-D integer indices of length nnz >= 1: an integer tensor, an integer numpy array, or a sequence of int or numpy integers. A set or a mapping is rejected, since entries pair up by position, and so is a complex tensor. Entry i is the input column of live edge i, and must satisfy 0 <= source_index < in_features. Copied to an int64 buffer, so later writes to the argument do not reach this layer.

required torch.Tensor, numpy.ndarray, or sequence of int

1-D integer indices of the same length, in the same forms as source_index. Entry i is the output row of live edge i, and must satisfy 0 <= target_index < out_features. The two arrays are paired position by position, must not repeat a (source, target) pair, and their shared order is also the order of weight.

required int or numpy integer

Width of the output axis. Must be a positive integer, stored as int. Note the order: out_features comes before in_features, as in the (out, in) shape of a dense weight, not in the nn.Linear argument order.

required int or numpy integer

Width of the input axis. Must be a positive integer, stored as int.

required bool

If True, learn a bias of shape (out_features,). If False, there is no bias. Must be a bool.

True str or None

Opaque checkpoint identity, typically spec.fingerprint. Stored in state_dict next to index_digest as a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of the UTF-8 bytes. load_state_dict compares it with the checkpoint's identity:

  • the checkpoint has no identity: it loads, even with strict=True
  • it has this layer's identity: it loads
  • it has another identity, or this layer's identity is None: Kpnn2Error, and no weights are loaded

None means this layer does not claim an identity, so it loads only checkpoints saved without one.

None Module or None

Optional per-entry map on the packed weight, applied in forward. The module must return a tensor of shape (nnz,). There are no absent edges here, so this map cannot resurrect a blocked cell. Give it a right_inverse (the torch.nn.utils.parametrize convention) and reset_parameters stores right_inverse(draw), so the effective weight keeps the degree-aware init; without one, weight stores the draw and the map is applied on top of it. nn.Softplus() is the textbook non-negative edge reparametrization but has no right_inverse: every edge then starts near ln 2 whatever its fan-in (see Notes). MaskedLinear takes the same argument. Mixed per-edge signs and frozen slots belong in this module, not in parse columns. A hard freeze is torch.where replacing those slots in forward; a gradient hook that zeroes grad[i] is not a freeze (AdamW and SGD with momentum still move the stored parameter).

None Generator or None

Isolated RNG for reset_parameters. None uses the default torch generator, bit-identical to omitting the argument. Not stored on the module; pass it again to reset_parameters to replay. Do not pass a seed integer.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description in_features int

Number of input columns.

out_features int

Number of output columns.

nnz int

Number of live edges, weight.shape[0].

weight Parameter

Trainable packed weights of shape (nnz,). One scalar per live edge, in the same order as the index buffers. This is an ordinary parameter; there is no dense (out, in) tensor. When constraint is set, this tensor is unconstrained. Read effective_weight() for the map forward uses. MaskedLinear.weight is stored the same way.

source_index Tensor

Int64 buffer of input columns, length nnz. Treat it as read-only: like any PyTorch buffer it can be written to, and doing so rewires the layer without reinitializing it. Rebuild from the edgelist instead.

target_index Tensor

Int64 buffer of output rows, length nnz, read-only in the same sense.

constraint Module or None

The constructor constraint module, or None.

bias Parameter | None

Trainable bias, or None when constructed with bias=False.

identity str | None

The constructor identity, or None.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If the indices are empty, not 1-D integers, mismatched in length, out of range, or duplicated as (source, target) pairs; if out_features / in_features are not positive integers; if bias is not a bool; if identity is neither a str nor None; if constraint is neither an nn.Module nor None, or does not preserve the packed weight shape; if generator is neither a torch.Generator nor None; from load_state_dict when the checkpoint carries an index digest or identity that does not match this layer, in which case the weights are not loaded; and from forward when x is not a floating-point tensor or its last dimension is not in_features.

See Also

MaskedLinear : Dense (out_features, in_features) weight; the GEMM hatch when that rectangle fits. Hop : One layer's packed edges on a LayeredSpec; pass it to from_hop. AdjacencySpec : Graph-wide packed edges; pass it to from_adjacency. PackedMultiheadAttention : Attention over the same packed pairs, when the update is a contraction rather than one scalar per edge. scatter_hop_outputs : Split a transposed hop's concatenated output back onto source layers. torch.nn.Linear : Dense equivalent, and the reference for shapes, bias, calling the module, and training.

Notes

Forward gathers x[..., source_index], multiplies by effective_weight() (constraint(weight) when constraint is set, else weight), and index_adds into zeros of shape (..., out_features), adding bias when present. x is an ordinary dense activation tensor whose last dimension must be in_features, as for nn.Linear. The gather reads columns by position, so a wider tensor would be read without complaint; forward raises instead. A stale align_inputs index of the same width after a reparse still cannot be detected here: recompute the index on the new spec. Nothing scatters into a dense (out, in) matrix, nothing imports torch.sparse, and no tensor subclass is involved, so torch.compile(layer, fullgraph=True) traces it. Index buffers stay integer after .half() / bfloat16 / .double(); weight and bias follow the module floating dtype like nn.Linear. torch.autocast is unsupported: forward disables it and casts a floating x to the parameter dtype so AMP cannot mix Half into index_add; an integer, bool, or complex x raises instead of being cast. Cast the module with .to(dtype=...) (or .half() / .double()) instead.

weight is the unconstrained tensor, so optimizer weight_decay pulls it toward 0. Under softplus that pulls the effective weight toward ln 2, not toward 0. Give a constrained layer weight_decay=0 in its param group and penalize effective_weight() in the loss instead. A right_inverse on the constraint keeps the degree-aware init; a constraint without one can initialize weight itself from init_bound().

reset_parameters uses per-row packed degree as fan_in, not full in_features. A row with fan_in == 0 has no packed weights and its bias stays 0; input nodes of an AdjacencySpec are exactly that case, and this layer does not invent identity connections for them. Optional generator isolates those draws from other torch RNG consumers.

state_dict keys are weight, optional bias, source_index, target_index, index_digest, and identity when the constructor was given one. index_digest is a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of length 32: the SHA-256 of the live index buffers' int64 C-contiguous bytes plus out_features and in_features as fixed-width integers, not a registered buffer. A missing digest is not an error, even with strict=True. The digest catches same-shape rewiring. A rename that leaves the packed index pattern unchanged is caught by identity when callers pass spec.fingerprint. copy.deepcopy works.

transpose() is the tied-autoencoder helper: it swaps the index buffers and the feature sizes so packed slot i is still the same live edge, then shares or copies weight and constraint together. Bias is never tied. Do not reparse a reversed edgelist and assign dec.weight = enc.weight: that permutes slots. On a hop whose source axis is several layers, split the transposed output with scatter_hop_outputs.

Examples:

An input feeding a two-node feedback core plus one output, stepped once over the shared state vector:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import torch
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["x", "a", "b", "a"],
...         "target": ["a", "b", "a", "y"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_adjacency(edgelist)
>>> core = kpnn2.PackedLinear.from_adjacency(
...     spec,
...     identity=spec.fingerprint,
... )
>>> core.in_features, core.out_features, core.nnz
(4, 4, 4)
>>> state = torch.zeros(2, spec.state_dim)
>>> state[:, spec.input_index] = torch.ones(2, 1)
>>> relu = torch.nn.ReLU()
>>> state = relu(core(state))
>>> tuple(state.shape)
(2, 4)
>>> tuple(state[:, spec.output_index].shape)
(2, 1)

The constructor takes packed indices that come from no spec, here two inputs feeding one output:

>>> layer = kpnn2.PackedLinear(
...     [0, 1],
...     [0, 0],
...     1,
...     2,
... )
>>> layer.nnz
2

docs.text:
from_hop(
    hop: Hop,
    bias: bool = True,
    *,
    identity: str | None = None,
    constraint: Module | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
) -> PackedLinear

Build the layer that applies one hop of a LayeredSpec.

This is the recommended way to build a PackedLinear on a hop. It reads the packed indices and both widths off hop, so source and target cannot be swapped by hand. A hand-written swap passes the constructor's range checks whenever the swapped indices still fit, which they always do when out_features == in_features; every edge then runs backwards. The result is the layer the constructor builds from hop.source_index, hop.target_index, hop.out_features, and hop.in_features, with the same init draws. It keeps no reference to hop.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default Hop

One entry of spec.hops from parse_layered.

required bool

Same as the PackedLinear constructor.

True str or None

Same as the PackedLinear constructor. A Hop does not carry the spec's fingerprint, so pass spec.fingerprint here yourself.

None Module or None

Same as the PackedLinear constructor.

None Generator or None

Same as the PackedLinear constructor.

None

Returns:

Type Description PackedLinear

New layer with in_features == hop.in_features, out_features == hop.out_features, and one weight per live edge of hop, in the hop's packed order.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If hop is not a Hop (a LayeredSpec or an AdjacencySpec included), or if the constructor rejects bias, identity, constraint, or generator.

See Also

PackedLinear.from_adjacency : The same on an AdjacencySpec. gather_hop_inputs : Builds the tensor this layer reads.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(
...     pd.DataFrame(
...         {
...             "source": ["A", "H", "A"],
...             "target": ["H", "C", "C"],
...         }
...     )
... )
>>> layer = kpnn2.PackedLinear.from_hop(
...     spec.hops[1],
...     identity=spec.fingerprint,
... )
>>> layer.out_features, layer.in_features, layer.nnz
(1, 2, 2)

The result is the layer the constructor builds from spec.source_index, spec.target_index, spec.state_dim, and spec.state_dim, with the same init draws. docs.title: effective_weight
docs.text:
effective_weight() -> torch.Tensor

Return the (nnz,) packed weights forward uses.

constraint(weight) when constraint is set, else weight itself. Recomputed on every call and differentiable, so it is the tensor to read, export, or penalize as the layer's live edge weights; index it with edge_location slots. MaskedLinear has the same method on its dense rectangle.

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The effective packed weights, one per live edge.

docs.title: init_bound
docs.text:
init_bound() -> torch.Tensor

Return the degree-aware init bound of every packed slot.

Slot i gets 1 / sqrt(fan_in) of its output row target_index[i], the bound reset_parameters draws that slot's effective weight from. Use it to initialize a constraint that has no right_inverse yourself. MaskedLinear has the same method on its rectangle.

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

Shape (nnz,), dtype and device of weight.

docs.title: reset_parameters
docs.text:
reset_parameters(
    generator: Generator | None = None,
) -> None

Initialize from per-row packed degree, not full width.

For output row j, fan_in is the number of packed edges with target_index == j (bincount, minlength=out_features). Each live edge into that row, and bias[j] if present, is drawn uniformly from [-1 / sqrt(fan_in), 1 / sqrt(fan_in)] (init_bound()). If fan_in == 0, that row has no packed weights and bias[j] stays 0.

The draw is the degree-aware value for the effective weight. Without constraint, or when constraint has no right_inverse, weight stores the draw itself. When constraint defines right_inverse (the torch.nn.utils.parametrize convention), weight stores constraint.right_inverse(draw), so effective_weight() keeps the degree-aware scale. The draws, and so the RNG stream, are the same either way.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default Generator or None

Isolated RNG for these draws. None uses the default torch generator. Not stored on the module.

None

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If generator is neither a torch.Generator nor None, or constraint.right_inverse returns a tensor of the wrong shape or a non-finite value.

docs.title: transpose
docs.text:
transpose(
    bias: bool = True,
    *,
    tie: bool = True,
    identity: str | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
) -> PackedLinear

Return a packed layer that applies the same edges backwards.

Packed slot i stays the same live edge: the 1-D weight is not permuted. The new layer reads the former output axis and writes the former input axis. That is the packed analogue of enc.weight.T for a tied autoencoder. With tie=True the whole live map is shared: weight and the constraint module. Bias is never shared.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bool

If True, the new layer gets its own bias of shape (in_features,), the original input width, initialized from the transposed packed degree. If False, there is no bias. This layer's bias is not copied. Must be a bool.

True bool

If True, the returned layer's weight is this layer's weight nn.Parameter, and its constraint is this layer's constraint module itself. Gradients from both forwards accumulate on the shared tensors, and a later change to the constraint's state (a pruning buffer written in place, a trained constraint parameter) reaches both layers, so the decoder always applies the transpose of the encoder's live map. If False, copy the current weight values into a new Parameter and deepcopy the constraint; the two layers are then independent. Must be a bool.

True str or None

Checkpoint identity for the new layer, typically spec.fingerprint. This layer's identity is not copied. None means the new layer does not claim an identity, so it loads only checkpoints saved without one.

None Generator or None

Forwarded to the inner PackedLinear constructor. None uses the default torch generator. A full init still runs, then weight is replaced; discarded weight draws still advance this generator.

None

Returns:

Type Description PackedLinear

New module: source_index and target_index swapped, in_features and out_features swapped, same nnz. constraint is this layer's constraint module when tie=True, a deepcopy of it when tie=False, or None. This layer and its constraint are not modified.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If bias or tie is not a bool, or if constructing the new layer fails (see the constructor).

Notes

Do not parse a reversed edgelist and assign dec.weight = enc.weight. Packed order is lexicographic by (source name, target name) of each spec, so those slots do not line up. This method keeps slot i as the same edge.

On a layered hop, the transposed output is hop.in_features wide. Split it with scatter_hop_outputs when the hop reads several source layers; add those pieces into the caller's saved dict, because two reversed hops may write the same earlier layer. An AdjacencySpec map is already n-wide; no gather or scatter.

MaskedLinear has no packed slots: use F.linear(h, layer.weight.T, dec_bias).

Examples:

Slot i is the same edge after a transpose, so sharing weight is the tied map:

>>> import torch
>>> import kpnn2
>>> layer = kpnn2.PackedLinear(
...     [0, 1],
...     [0, 0],
...     1,
...     2,
...     bias=False,
... )
>>> with torch.no_grad():
...     layer.weight[:] = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0])
>>> mirrored = layer.transpose(bias=False)
>>> mirrored.weight is layer.weight
True
>>> mirrored.in_features, mirrored.out_features
(1, 2)
>>> layer(torch.tensor([[1.0, 4.0]])).tolist()
[[14.0]]
>>> mirrored(torch.tensor([[1.0]])).tolist()
[[2.0, 3.0]]

docs.title: forward
docs.text:
forward(x: Tensor) -> torch.Tensor

Gather live inputs, scale by packed weights, index_add.

contrib = x[..., source_index] * effective_weight(), then index_add into zeros of shape (..., out_features). Adds bias when present. Packed 1-D weights, one per live edge; not torch.sparse; forward is index_add. torch.autocast is unsupported: this path disables it and casts x to the parameter dtype.

Raises Kpnn2Error when x is not a floating-point tensor or its last dimension is not in_features. An integer, bool, or complex x is rejected, not cast.

docs.title: PackedMultiheadAttention
docs.text:
PackedMultiheadAttention(
    source_index: object,
    target_index: object,
    query_features: int,
    key_features: int,
    embed_dim: int,
    num_heads: int,
    dropout: float = 0.0,
    bias: bool = True,
    kdim: int | None = None,
    vdim: int | None = None,
    batch_first: bool = True,
    add_self_loops: bool = False,
    *,
    identity: str | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
    chunk_size: int | None = None,
)

Bases: Module

Multi-head attention in which each node attends only to its sources.

Prior knowledge decides who may attend to whom; the data decides how much. Every node is one token, a vector of embed_dim numbers that stands for the node inside your model. For each node, the layer looks at the nodes with an edge into it (its sources), weighs them by how well their tokens match its own, and returns a weighted mix of what they pass on. The weights are recomputed for every sample: with a gene-regulatory prior, a target gene can weigh its regulators differently in each cell, depending on their state and its own. Two nodes without an edge exchange nothing in this layer.

Information flows along the edge arrow, from source to target, as in PackedLinear. In attention terms, the target asks and its sources answer. The target's token gives a query (what it looks for). Each source's token gives a key (what it offers to be matched against) and a value (what it passes on). Each query-key pair, that is, each live edge, gets a score. A softmax over the edges into one node turns their scores into weights that are non-negative and sum to 1, so the sources compete: a higher weight for one leaves less for the others. num_heads such weightings run side by side, each on its own slice of the channels, so different heads can weigh the same sources differently.

Compare PackedLinear, which learns one weight per edge, fixed after training and the same for every sample. Here nothing is learned per edge. The learned parameters are four embed_dim x embed_dim projections shared by every node and edge (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, out_proj), so their number does not depend on the graph. The graph only decides which pairs are scored.

One call moves information one edge along the graph: a node's output depends only on its own token and those of its direct sources. Stack layers in your own encoder to reach nodes further upstream. This layer is that one building block, not a Transformer. You build the tokens (for example a projection of each measured value plus a learned embedding per node) and write the rest around the layer: normalization, residual connections, a feed-forward network, and the readout.

Masking nn.MultiheadAttention with the graph computes the same mix for every node that has a source. But it scores every pair of tokens, an (n, n) matrix per head and sample (400 million scores for 20,000 nodes), and then discards the pairs without an edge. This layer scores only the live edges, so its memory and time grow with their number, nnz, rather than with n squared.

Build it with from_adjacency on a parse_adjacency spec: one token per node (per unit, when widths= gives a node several). It reads the indices and sequence lengths off the spec, so the query and key sides cannot be swapped by hand. The constructor below takes packed indices directly, for pairs that come from no spec, such as a bipartite map in which pathway tokens (queries) attend to gene tokens (keys).

Call it like nn.MultiheadAttention (it is not a subclass): layer(query, key, value), passing the same tokens three times for attention within one graph. Two defaults differ from MHA: batch_first=True and need_weights=False. With need_weights=True the layer returns one weight per live edge, not a dense (L, S) matrix.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default torch.Tensor, numpy.ndarray, or sequence of int

Where each live edge starts. Entry i is the position in key / value of the token that edge i reads from, and must satisfy 0 <= source_index < key_features. 1-D integer indices of length nnz >= 1: an integer tensor, an integer numpy array, or a sequence of int or numpy integers. A set or a mapping is rejected, since entries pair up by position, and so is a complex tensor. Copied to an int64 buffer, so later writes to the argument do not reach this layer.

required torch.Tensor, numpy.ndarray, or sequence of int

Where each live edge ends. Entry i is the position in query of the token that attends along edge i, and must satisfy 0 <= target_index < query_features. Same length and forms as source_index. The two arrays are paired position by position and must not repeat a (source, target) pair. Their shared order is the order of the per-edge weights forward returns; pairs added by add_self_loops follow at the end.

required int or numpy integer

How many tokens attend: the sequence length of query. Positive integer, stored as int.

required int or numpy integer

How many tokens can be attended to: the sequence length of key / value. Positive integer, stored as int. Equal to query_features for attention within one node set; smaller or larger for a bipartite query/key map.

required int or numpy integer

How many numbers describe each token: the width of query, key, value, and the output. A wider token can carry more about its node, and the four projections hold 4 * embed_dim**2 weights. Positive integer, divisible by num_heads, stored as int.

required int or numpy integer

How many attention patterns run side by side. Each head scores the same live edges from its own embed_dim // num_heads channels, so it can weigh a node's sources differently from the other heads. The heads' mixes are joined and passed through out_proj. Positive integer, stored as int.

required float

Regularization on the edge weights, in training mode only: each weight is zeroed with this probability and the rest are scaled by 1 / (1 - dropout), so the model cannot lean on any single edge. 0.0 disables it. Must be finite and in [0, 1], the range torch accepts; integers 0 and 1 are accepted, bool is rejected.

0.0 bool

Whether the four projections learn an additive bias. False makes them pure linear maps. Must be a bool.

True int, numpy integer, or None

Exists so code written for nn.MultiheadAttention runs unchanged; keys of a different width are not supported. Must be None or an int or numpy integer equal to embed_dim (True is rejected even when embed_dim is 1).

None int, numpy integer, or None

Same as kdim, for the values.

None bool

Where the batch axis sits. True (kpnn2 sample-major): batched tensors are (..., seq, embed_dim). False (the nn.MultiheadAttention layout): batched tensors are (seq, batch, embed_dim). Unbatched 2-D (seq, embed_dim) ignores this flag. Must be a bool.

True bool

Let every token also attend to itself. Without a self-loop, a node's own token shapes how it weighs its sources (through its query) but is not part of the mix, and a node with no incoming edge, such as an input node of an AdjacencySpec, mixes to zeros. With True, any missing (i, i) pair is added to this layer's index buffers, after the given pairs. Existing self-loops are kept, not duplicated, and the caller's index objects are not mutated. The graph itself is not changed: other layers built from the same spec do not see these pairs. Requires query_features == key_features. Must be a bool.

False str or None

Labels the graph this layer belongs to, so load_state_dict refuses a checkpoint labeled for another graph, even one with the same index pattern, such as a graph with a renamed node. Typically spec.fingerprint. An opaque string, stored in state_dict next to index_digest as a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of the UTF-8 bytes. load_state_dict compares it with the checkpoint's identity:

  • the checkpoint has no identity: it loads, even with strict=True
  • it has this layer's identity: it loads
  • it has another identity, or this layer's identity is None: Kpnn2Error, and no weights are loaded

None means this layer does not claim an identity, so it loads only checkpoints saved without one.

None Generator or None

A reproducible start without touching the global random state: the Xavier-uniform draws for the four projections use this generator. None uses the default torch generator and keeps today's path: nn.Linear kaiming-init then Xavier on that global stream. When set, those nn.Linear constructors do not advance the global stream. Not stored on the module; pass it again to reset_parameters to replay. Do not pass a seed integer.

None int, numpy integer, or None

Memory control for large graphs; it does not change what is computed. None gathers all live edges at once. A positive int processes them in slices of that many edges, so training holds less memory, at the cost of time: the softmax is still over every live key of a query, but the pair gathers are slices, and backward recomputes them. With a positive int, forward and backward also check on every call that each query's packed softmax sums to 1 (to 0 only when no live key scores above -inf: none left after padding, or every score overflowed) and that its gradient sums to 0, and raise AssertionError (a kpnn2 bug) if not; each check waits for the device once. A numpy integer is stored as int. bool and values other than None or a positive integer raise Kpnn2Error. Not stored in state_dict or index_digest, so a checkpoint loads into a layer with another chunk_size.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description query_features int

Number of tokens that attend (sequence length of query).

key_features int

Number of tokens that can be attended to (sequence length of key / value).

embed_dim int

Token width.

num_heads int

Number of attention heads.

head_dim int

Channels per head, embed_dim // num_heads.

nnz int

Number of live edges scored, counting any pair added by add_self_loops.

dropout float

Dropout probability on the edge weights.

batch_first bool

Layout flag; default True.

add_self_loops bool

Whether missing self-loops were added at construction.

source_index Tensor

Int64 buffer: the key / value position of each live edge, length nnz. Treat it as read-only: like any PyTorch buffer it can be written to, and doing so rewires the layer without reinitializing it. Rebuild from the edgelist instead.

target_index Tensor

Int64 buffer: the query position of each live edge, length nnz, read-only in the same sense.

q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, out_proj Linear

The four learned embed_dim -> embed_dim projections (query, key, value, and output): separate layers, not a fused in_proj_weight.

identity str | None

The constructor identity, or None.

chunk_size int | None

Edge-chunk length, or None for all live edges at once.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

At construction, if the indices are empty, not 1-D integers, mismatched in length, out of range, or duplicated as (source, target) pairs; if the sizes are not positive integers; if embed_dim is not divisible by num_heads; if dropout is a bool, not a number, NaN, or outside [0, 1]; if bias, batch_first, or add_self_loops is not a bool; if kdim / vdim are neither None nor an integer equal to embed_dim; if add_self_loops is set when query_features != key_features; if identity is neither a str nor None; if generator is neither a torch.Generator nor None; or if chunk_size is neither None nor a positive integer. From load_state_dict, when the checkpoint carries an index digest or identity that does not match this layer, in which case the weights are not loaded. forward documents its own rejected arguments.

See Also

PackedLinear : Same packed pairs, but one trained weight per edge, the same for every sample, instead of attention weights computed per sample. MaskedLinear : Dense (out, in) weight; the default layer whenever that square fits. AdjacencySpec : Graph-wide packed edges; pass it to from_adjacency. torch.nn.MultiheadAttention : Dense equivalent, and the reference for call shape, heads, and training.

Notes

One forward pass, for one sample and one head with d = embed_dim // num_heads channels:

  1. Project every token: q = q_proj(query), k = k_proj(key), v = v_proj(value), each split into num_heads slices of d channels.
  2. Score each live edge e from source s to target t: score[e] = dot(q[t], k[s]) / sqrt(d).
  3. Turn the scores of the edges into each target into weights with a softmax over those edges only. Keys masked by key_padding_mask take no part. In training mode, dropout then zeroes weights at random and scales the rest by 1 / (1 - dropout).
  4. Mix: mixed[t] is the sum of weight[e] * v[s] over the edges e into t.
  5. Join the heads' slices of mixed back into embed_dim channels and apply out_proj.

A query with no live keys, because it has no incoming edge and no self-loop or because key_padding_mask removed all of them, mixes to zeros rather than NaN, so its output is the bias of out_proj (zeros when bias=False). Input nodes of an AdjacencySpec are exactly that case unless add_self_loops=True. With it, an input node's only key is itself, so its softmax weight is 1 and it passes on its own value.

No (n, n) or (L, S) score matrix is ever allocated and torch.sparse is not imported; cost scales with nnz, not with query_features * key_features. chunk_size=None (the default) gathers all live pairs at once, and training keeps those (..., nnz, heads, head_dim) gathers for backward. A positive chunk_size gathers chunked live pairs and rematerializes those (..., chunk, heads, head_dim) tensors in backward, so training does not save a full (..., nnz, heads, head_dim) gather. The packed softmax (..., nnz, heads) is still stored.

forward documents the accepted layouts, packed need_weights, attn_mask / is_causal, and key_padding_mask.

Index buffers stay integer after .half() / bfloat16 / .double(); projection weights follow the module floating dtype like nn.Linear. torch.autocast is unsupported: forward disables it and casts query, key, and value to the parameter dtype. They must be floating-point tensors; an integer, bool, or complex input raises instead of being cast. Cast the module with .to(dtype=...) (or .half() / .double()) instead.

state_dict adds index_digest, a 1-D CPU uint8 tensor of length 32: the SHA-256 of the packed indices plus query_features, key_features, embed_dim, and num_heads, so a reshape or a different head split cannot collide. It is not a registered buffer, and a missing digest is not an error, even with strict=True. identity is stored the same way when the constructor was given one: a rename that leaves the packed index pattern unchanged is caught when callers pass spec.fingerprint. chunk_size is not part of state_dict or index_digest. copy.deepcopy works.

Examples:

An input x feeds a two-node feedback loop between a and b, which feeds an output y. All four nodes form one four-token sequence:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import torch
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["x", "a", "b", "a"],
...         "target": ["a", "b", "a", "y"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_adjacency(edgelist)
>>> attn = kpnn2.PackedMultiheadAttention.from_adjacency(
...     spec,
...     embed_dim=8,
...     num_heads=2,
...     add_self_loops=True,
...     identity=spec.fingerprint,
... )
>>> attn.nnz, attn.head_dim
(8, 4)
>>> tokens = torch.randn(2, spec.state_dim, 8)
>>> output, weights = attn(tokens, tokens, tokens)
>>> tuple(output.shape)
(2, 4, 8)
>>> weights is None
True

With need_weights=True each sample gets one weight per live edge: the four graph edges, then the four added self-loops.

>>> _, packed = attn(
...     tokens,
...     tokens,
...     tokens,
...     need_weights=True,
... )
>>> tuple(packed.shape)
(2, 8)
>>> for s, t in zip(
...     attn.source_index.tolist(),
...     attn.target_index.tolist(),
... ):
...     print(spec.nodes[s], "->", spec.nodes[t])
a -> b
a -> y
b -> a
x -> a

b -> b
x -> x

docs.title: from_adjacency classmethod
docs.text:
from_adjacency(
    spec: AdjacencySpec,
    embed_dim: int,
    num_heads: int,
    *,
    dropout: float = 0.0,
    bias: bool = True,
    batch_first: bool = True,
    add_self_loops: bool = False,
    identity: str | None = None,
    generator: Generator | None = None,
    chunk_size: int | None = None,
) -> PackedMultiheadAttention

Build attention over the nodes of an AdjacencySpec.

This is the recommended way to build this layer on an AdjacencySpec: one token per unit of the state vector, and the query at each edge's target attends to the key at its source. It reads the packed indices off spec and uses spec.state_dim as both sequence lengths, so the query and key sides cannot be swapped by hand. On this square layout a hand-written swap is always silent: the constructor accepts it and every node attends along reversed edges. The result is the layer the constructor builds from spec.source_index, spec.target_index, spec.state_dim, spec.state_dim, embed_dim, and num_heads, with the same init draws. It keeps no reference to spec. Options after num_heads are keyword-only; kdim and vdim, which can only equal embed_dim, are left out.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default AdjacencySpec

Spec from parse_adjacency.

required int or numpy integer

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

required int or numpy integer

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

required float

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

0.0 bool

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

True bool

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

True bool

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

False str or None

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor. Not filled in from spec: pass spec.fingerprint yourself.

None Generator or None

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

None int, numpy integer, or None

Same as the PackedMultiheadAttention constructor.

None

Returns:

Type Description PackedMultiheadAttention

New layer with query_features == key_features == spec.state_dim.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If spec is not an AdjacencySpec (a LayeredSpec or a Hop included), or if the constructor rejects any other argument.

See Also

PackedLinear.from_adjacency : One trainable scalar per edge on the same packed pairs.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_adjacency(
...     pd.DataFrame(
...         {
...             "source": ["x", "a", "b", "a"],
...             "target": ["a", "b", "a", "y"],
...         }
...     )
... )
>>> attn = kpnn2.PackedMultiheadAttention.from_adjacency(
...     spec,
...     embed_dim=8,
...     num_heads=2,
...     identity=spec.fingerprint,
... )
>>> attn.query_features, attn.key_features, attn.nnz
(4, 4, 4)

docs.title: forward
docs.text:
forward(
    query: Tensor,
    key: Tensor,
    value: Tensor,
    key_padding_mask: Tensor | None = None,
    need_weights: bool = False,
    attn_mask: Tensor | None = None,
    average_attn_weights: bool = True,
    is_causal: bool = False,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor | None]

Let each query attend to its live keys and mix their values.

For attention within one graph, pass the same tokens as query, key, and value: every node then attends to its sources. Pass different tensors when queries and keys are different token sets, as in a bipartite map built with the constructor. The arguments are those of nn.MultiheadAttention.forward, so an encoder written for it can call this layer; the class docstring lists the differences.

With batch_first=True (the default), query, key, and value are (..., seq, embed_dim): unbatched 2-D (seq, embed_dim), batched 3-D (batch, seq, embed_dim), or more leading axes. With batch_first=False, unbatched 2-D is still (seq, embed_dim); batched 3-D is (seq, batch, embed_dim), transposed to batch-first for the packed kernel and transposed back. The batch axes of all three must match.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default Tensor

The tokens that attend: query_features of them along the sequence axis, each embed_dim wide. Must be floating-point; an integer, bool, or complex tensor raises Kpnn2Error rather than being cast to the parameter dtype.

required Tensor

The tokens matched against the queries: key_features of them along the sequence axis, each embed_dim wide. Floating-point, like query. Required; it is not defaulted to query.

required Tensor

What each key position passes on, in the shape of key and usually the same tensor. Floating-point, like query.

required Tensor or None

Keys to leave out of a given sample, for example a feature that sample did not measure: True means ignore that key. Its edges drop out of the softmax, so each query's remaining sources share the whole weight. A boolean tensor of shape (S,) unbatched or (N, S) batched, where S = key_features; with more leading axes, the same ones as the batch-first query. The batch axes come first even when batch_first=False. Applied in packed space, without allocating (n, n). Copied onto the scores' device and kept boolean. A float mask raises Kpnn2Error.

None bool

Also return the weight of every live edge, for example to draw edge thickness on the prior graph. Must be a bool.

False Tensor or None

Must be None: the edgelist is the mask. Kept so that calls written for nn.MultiheadAttention still run.

None bool

With need_weights=True: True averages the weights over the heads, False keeps one per head. Must be a bool.

True bool

Must be False. Kept so that calls written for nn.MultiheadAttention still run.

False

Returns:

Name Type Description output Tensor

The updated tokens, one per query position, in the shape and layout of query. A query with no live keys left mixes to zeros, not NaN, before out_proj.

weights Tensor or None

None unless need_weights=True. Then the softmax weight of every live edge, in the order of source_index / target_index, not nn.MultiheadAttention's dense (L, S) map; this path does not allocate (L, S). Shape (..., nnz) averaged over heads, or (..., nnz, num_heads) per head, with the batch axes placed as in output: (nnz, batch) or (nnz, batch, num_heads) when batch_first=False and the input is batched. The weights into one query sum to 1, or to 0 when it has no live key. In training mode with dropout > 0 they are the weights after dropout, as the mix used them; call eval() first to read the plain softmax. nnz counts the pairs added by add_self_loops, so zip the weights with this layer's source_index / target_index, not with to_edgelist().

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If query, key, or value is not a floating-point tensor of at least 2 dimensions with last axis embed_dim and the sequence length above; if their batch axes differ; if a batched input is not 3-D under batch_first=False; if key_padding_mask is not a boolean tensor of the shape above; if need_weights or average_attn_weights is not a bool; if attn_mask is not None; or if is_causal is not False.

docs.title: Skip dataclass
docs.text:
Skip(
    source: str,
    target: str,
    source_layer: int,
    target_layer: int,
    source_in_layer: int,
    target_in_layer: int,
)

One original edge whose endpoints are more than one layer apart.

Metadata, not a second computation: the named edge is already a block of packed unit pairs in LayeredSpec.hops[target_layer - 1], exactly like an adjacent edge, so nothing has to add it back later and nothing can forget to. Read LayeredSpec.skips to inspect which prior-knowledge edges span layers; a forward pass never reads it. parse_layered builds these, never the caller.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default str

Name of the node the edge leaves, as it appears in LayeredSpec.layer_nodes[source_layer].

required str

Name of the node the edge enters, as it appears in LayeredSpec.layer_nodes[target_layer].

required int

Depth of source: its index into LayeredSpec.layer_nodes.

required int

Depth of target. Always at least two above source_layer; that gap is what makes the edge a skip, and it names the hop carrying it, hops[target_layer - 1].

required int

First unit of source inside its layer (the block start). At width 1 this equals the node's index in layer_nodes[source_layer]. It is not a column of the hop's concatenated source axis. LayeredSpec.edge_location returns the packed slots.

required int

First unit of target inside its layer (the block start). At width 1 this equals the node's index in layer_nodes[target_layer]. Locating the skip among packed indices means every unit pair in that block is live, not a single (column, row) pair. Use LayeredSpec.edge_location.

required See Also

Hop : The packed edges this skip is already one of, alongside every other parent of target_layer. LayeredSpec : Holds skips, empty when no edge spans layers. parse_layered : Builds the spec these records come from.

Notes

Every original edge with a depth gap greater than 1 is recorded once; adjacent edges never are. Membership changes nothing about how the edge is computed: its weight, the unit bias, and the fan-in the degree-aware initialization uses all stay on the target layer's PackedLinear or MaskedLinear. Expanding a skip into dummy neurons is not the intended use. At width greater than 1 the stored indices are block starts; every unit pair of that block is a packed index of the hop.

Examples:

Locate a skip among packed indices. This graph is width 1, so the skip is one packed pair:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["A", "B", "H", "A"],
...         "target": ["H", "H", "C", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> skip = spec.skips[0]
>>> skip.source, skip.target
('A', 'C')
>>> skip.source_layer, skip.target_layer
(0, 2)
>>> hop_index, packed = spec.edge_location(
...     skip.source,
...     skip.target,
... )
>>> hop_index
1
>>> packed
(0,)

docs.title: align_inputs
docs.text:
align_inputs(
    names: object,
    spec: LayeredSpec | AdjacencySpec,
) -> np.ndarray

Return an integer index that orders features to spec inputs.

The columns of a feature table rarely come in the order of spec.input_nodes, which the parsed edgelist fixes. The model reads columns by position, not by name, so a column in the wrong place feeds the wrong input node without any error. This returns a 1-D int64 index into the caller's feature axis; indexing that axis with it puts the columns in input-node order. It does not take the matrix, copy sample rows, or densify. Apply the index on whatever holds X: X[:, col] for numpy, scipy CSR/CSC, AnnData .X in those formats, or a tensor; df.to_numpy()[:, col] for a DataFrame. COO-style sparse layouts do not support integer column indexing; convert first. Input nodes always have width 1, so the index has one position per input node. Call it after parsing, once, instead of hand-ordering columns. Pass the names, not the data: DataFrames, tensors, and matrices are rejected.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sequence of labels

The feature names, one per column, in the order the columns sit in your data: df.columns, adata.var_names, a 1-D numpy array, or a list. The annotated type is object because a DataFrame or tensor passed here by mistake is rejected at runtime. Names are compared to node names as text, after the same str(...) conversion edgelist nodes go through, so an integer 1 matches node "1". Names that are not graph nodes are ignored, so extra columns are fine. A name of a hidden or output node raises, because the model computes that node and would never read the column. Neither names nor the matrix is modified.

required LayeredSpec or AdjacencySpec

Parsed edgelist whose input_nodes — the in-degree-0 nodes, alphabetically sorted — fix both the required names and their order.

required

Returns:

Type Description numpy.ndarray of dtype int64, shape (len(spec.input_nodes),)

Positions into names, one per input node in spec.input_nodes order. That length is spec.layer_dims[0] for a LayeredSpec and len(spec.input_index) for an AdjacencySpec. Index the caller's feature axis with it. An empty names sequence is allowed when input_nodes is empty; otherwise missing names raise.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If spec is neither a LayeredSpec nor an AdjacencySpec; names is a DataFrame, tensor, string, bytes, mapping, set, AnnData-like object, or a matrix (ndim ≠ 1); names is not a sequence of labels; labels are duplicated (including after str conversion; the message names the unique duplicated labels, sorted, comma-separated); required names are missing (the message names them, sorted, and counts the input nodes found); or a name matches a hidden or output node (the message names each with its role, sorted). Missing names and computed-node names are reported in one message.

See Also

parse_layered : Builds the LayeredSpec whose input_nodes set this column order. parse_adjacency : Builds the AdjacencySpec for the packed layout, where the result needs scattering first. gather_hop_inputs : Assembles a later hop's input; layer 0 comes from indexing with this result instead.

Notes

Call it for every feature table, including one whose columns already follow spec.input_nodes: it is the one check that the data match the graph's input nodes by name.

Input nodes are not declared; they are the nodes with no incoming edge. The edgelist therefore starts at the measured features, one input node per feature column, named like that column. Name measured features so no computed node shares a name, for example STAT3_gene for the gene and STAT3 for the transcription factor node. Then an edgelist that starts at the first computed layer, which makes those computed nodes inputs, raises here as missing names. One name is one node, so a feature named like a hidden or output node has no input node of its own, and that raises too. With shared names, such as transcription factor nodes named by gene symbol beside a table of every gene, an edgelist that starts at a computed layer can match feature columns and pass.

AnnData, numpy matrices, and scipy sparse matrices are not accepted as names; pass the labels that sit on that axis and apply the index on the matrix. scipy CSR/CSC and AnnData .X in those formats stay sparse under X[:, col] until the caller densifies one row block. COO and similar layouts cannot be indexed that way.

hops[0] of a LayeredSpec reads layer 0 alone, so a row block indexed with this result feeds the first hop directly and needs no gathering. For an AdjacencySpec the returned length is not the state width: to_mask() is (state_dim, state_dim) over every node's units, while the index covers the input units only (len(spec.input_index)). Scatter the gathered columns into the spec.state_dim-wide state vector with state.index_copy(-1, input_index, x) before calling MaskedLinear(spec.to_mask()). input_index is a buffer, torch.as_tensor(spec.input_index).

Examples:

Names that are not graph nodes are ignored, and the rest are reordered:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["A", "H"],
...         "target": ["H", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> spec.input_nodes
('A',)
>>> names = ["unused", "A"]
>>> col = kpnn2.align_inputs(names, spec)
>>> col.dtype
dtype('int64')
>>> col.tolist()
[1]
>>> values = np.array([[9.0, 0.5], [8.0, 1.5]])
>>> values[:, col].tolist()
[[0.5], [1.5]]

An AdjacencySpec works the same way, but the index is len(spec.input_index) long and the gathered columns must be scattered into the state vector before they reach MaskedLinear(spec.to_mask()):

>>> import torch
>>> cyclic = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["x", "a", "b", "a"],
...         "target": ["a", "b", "a", "y"],
...     }
... )
>>> state_spec = kpnn2.parse_adjacency(cyclic)
>>> col = kpnn2.align_inputs(["x"], state_spec)
>>> col.tolist(), tuple(state_spec.to_mask().shape)
([0], (4, 4))
>>> x = torch.tensor([[0.5], [1.5]])[:, col]
>>> state = torch.zeros(
...     2,
...     state_spec.state_dim,
... )
>>> index = torch.as_tensor(state_spec.input_index)
>>> state = state.index_copy(
...     -1,
...     index,
...     x,
... )
>>> state.tolist()
[[0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, 1.5, 0.0]]

A feature named like a node the model computes raises, because its column would never be read:

>>> computed = ["A", "H"]
>>> kpnn2.align_inputs(computed, spec)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
Kpnn2Error: Feature names match node(s) the model computes, ...

A tensor is not accepted; pass the names that label it:

>>> t = torch.tensor([[0.5], [1.5]])
>>> kpnn2.align_inputs(t, spec)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
Kpnn2Error: 'names' is a tensor; pass the feature names that ...

Names you call or construct.

Name Description parse_layered Parse a source/target edgelist into a LayeredSpec (DAG only; optional widths=, ranks=). parse_adjacency Parse a source/target edgelist into an AdjacencySpec (packed layout; cycles allowed). PackedMultiheadAttention Attention that scores only live edgelist pairs, not a full matrix. gather_hop_inputs Build the input for one hop from the layer activations you saved. scatter_hop_outputs Split a tensor laid out like one hop's input back into its layers. align_inputs Feature names → column index so the wiring matches. map_node_attributions Attach spec node names to an attribution tensor you already computed. aggregate_node_attributions Reduce mapped node scores with a registered method (default rauter_mangano_2026 is not yet implemented). list_aggregation_methods Table of registered attribution aggregation methods and their status.

Returned by the parsers. Frozen dataclasses; densify with to_mask() when you need a rectangle.

Name Description LayeredSpec A DAG as named layers and packed hops; not a ready-made model. Hop Incoming packed wiring of one layer; pass it to PackedLinear.from_hop(). Skip Record of an edge that jumps layers; already a packed pair of its hop. AdjacencySpec Every node in one state vector, with packed edges; pass it to PackedLinear.from_adjacency().

docs.title: gather_hop_inputs
docs.text:
gather_hop_inputs(
    saved: Mapping[int, Tensor],
    hop: Hop,
) -> torch.Tensor

Build one hop's input from the layer activations you saved.

Without skip edges, each layer reads only the layer directly below it, so one module's output is the next module's input. A skip edge breaks that chain: its source sits two or more layers below its target. kpnn2 still applies every edge into a layer with one module, the one built from that layer's hop (PackedLinear.from_hop(hop) or MaskedLinear(hop.to_mask())). That module therefore needs every layer its target's parents sit in, at once and as one tensor. This function builds that tensor. It does no arithmetic; it only arranges tensors you already have.

Take A and B feeding H, H feeding C, and the skip A -> C. Layer 0 is [A, B], layer 1 is [H], and the hop into C reads both, so its input is the three columns [A, B, H]: whole layers, laid side by side in depth order. B is among them although there is no edge B -> C. The hop says which layers to read, in which order, and how many units wide each must be. Without skip edges, every hop reads a single layer, and that layer is the input as it stands.

Precisely, a hop's source columns are whole source layers laid side by side, so the tensor feeding PackedLinear or MaskedLinear on that hop is those layers concatenated. Call it between hops, keeping every layer you produce in saved; a forgotten layer raises rather than dropping the edges that read it. Inputs are never modified, and a single-source hop returns the saved tensor itself.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mapping of int to torch.Tensor

Layer depth to that layer's activation, as far as forward() has produced them. saved[i] is shaped (..., layer_dims[i]); the leading dimensions are the caller's, typically a batch. Only the layers in hop.source_layers are read, so extra keys are ignored, and those layers must share a dtype, a device, and their leading dimensions. Neither the mapping nor its tensors are copied or modified.

required Hop

The hop about to be applied, one entry of spec.hops. Its source_layers and source_dims decide which keys are read, in which order, and how wide each one must be; the packed indices are not used here.

required

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The hop's source axis, shape (..., hop.in_features), columns in concatenated source-unit order, dtype and device of the saved layers. source_nodes is one name per node, so it is shorter than this axis when a source node is wider than 1. When the hop reads a single layer, including hops[0] and any hop whose parents all sit at one depth, this is that saved tensor itself rather than a copy, so writing into it writes into the saved activation.

Raises:

Type Description Kpnn2Error

If saved is not a mapping or hop is not a Hop; a layer in hop.source_layers is absent from saved or is not a tensor; a saved tensor is 0-dimensional or is the wrong number of units wide; or the source layers disagree on dtype, device, or a dimension other than the last, such as the batch size.

See Also

scatter_hop_outputs : Split the concatenated axis this returns back onto source layers. PackedLinear : Applies the hop to the tensor returned here. PackedLinear.transpose : Tied decode of that hop; feed its output to scatter_hop_outputs when the hop reads several layers. MaskedLinear : Dense hatch via hop.to_mask(). Hop : The record that fixes the source layers and the concatenated column order this follows. align_inputs : Column index that puts named features in the order layer 0 expects.

Notes

Nothing here is graph-aware: this holds no weights, does not inject values into the previous layer, and does not pick skip sources by name. Columns that are not edges stay in the concatenated tensor; PackedLinear never reads them, and MaskedLinear(hop.to_mask()) zeros them. In the [A, B, H] example above, the A -> C weight is the packed pair whose source column is A.

An AdjacencySpec has no hops and is not accepted; in that layout every edge is already a packed index pair.

Examples:

The hop into C reads layers 0 and 1, so its input is two columns wide:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import torch
>>> import kpnn2
>>> edgelist = pd.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "source": ["A", "H", "A"],
...         "target": ["H", "C", "C"],
...     }
... )
>>> spec = kpnn2.parse_layered(edgelist)
>>> saved = {
...     0: torch.tensor([[2.0]]),
...     1: torch.tensor([[5.0]]),
... }
>>> x = kpnn2.gather_hop_inputs(
...     saved,
...     spec.hops[1],
... )
>>> x.tolist()
[[2.0, 5.0]]

Forgetting to store a layer raises instead of silently dropping the edges that read it:

>>> kpnn2.gather_hop_inputs(
...     {1: torch.tensor([[5.0]])},
...     spec.hops[1],
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
Kpnn2Error: saved is missing layer 0. ...

map_node_attributions(
